newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Violence sown in SAfrica's KwaZulu-Natal -Mandela.
newsitem.headline: Violence sown in SAfrica's KwaZulu-Natal -Mandela.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela said on Sunday that despite the peace process taking root in South Africa's troubled KwaZulu-Natal province, members of the security forces continued to instigate and fuel violence.
Mandela was speaking in the picturesque KwaZulu-Natal town of Richmond at the funeral of five African National Congress members recently shot dead, execution style.

He told thousands of mourners, gathered around the five coffins -- painted green, yellow and black in the colours of the ruling ANC -- that a few security force members were derailing the good work of the majority of the army and the police.

"We are dealing with experienced political criminals in command of huge resources -- finances, weaponry, communications networks and connections at key positions. We are dealing with a highly co-ordinated network of people deployed in state organs such as the army and police," Mandela said.

"They will not succeed. We are determined, together with the overwhelming majority of our security forces, the army, the police and the intelligence community, to root out the third force network," he added.
About 600 hundred troops were present at the funeral as fears of further violence in the strife-torn area abounded.
The five victims, including two recently elected ANC councillors, were shot dead execution-style by gunmen two days after a by-election in the area on July 20.
Police found the bodies on Wednesday, July 23 and said then that the attack appeared to be politically motivated.
Violence monitors identified the area as a hotspot after ANC leader Sifiso Nkabinde was thrown out of the party earlier this year on allegations of spying for the former white government.
His expulsion was followed by the resignation of a group of ANC councillors who wanted to show their support for Nkabinde, a self-confessed warlord.
Nkabinde has joined forces with former ANC member Bantu Holomisa who has formed the National Consultative Forum (NCF). Nkabinde is the party's KwaZulu-Natal chairman.
In the recent by-election the ANC won four of the five wards in Richmond with significant majorities. The NCF won one ward.
All the newly elected councillors have been placed under a 24-hour police guard as investigations continue.

The investigation team led by Director Bushie Engelbrecht, who was personally appointed by Mandela, has severed all ties with local policing structures after allegations that some policemen may have been involved in the killings.

"The special investigation unit is making progress and the government will give the unit all the support it needs...However, there remains a tiny minority of traitors within the security forces," Mandela said in Richmond, about 80 km (50 miles) west of the Indian Ocean port of Durban.

Safety and Security Minister Sydney Mufamadi has said allegations of police complicity in violence in the area would be probed by an independent complaints directorate and that some senior officers would be redeployed to other areas.
Mandela said that his government has achieved a sharp reduction in political violence in KwaZulu-Natal.
"The wounds of the past conflict are beginning to heal," he told the mourners, among them his former wife Winnie Mandela who is president of the ANC's Women's League.
